doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

chapter: Teaching, studio work and race in New York
title: Ignoring criticism of free jazz and the rules; a teacher's remark
summary: Asked about the sneer that free jazz is for those who can't play, he says he ignored rules, recalling a substitute teacher's remark about Negroes.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Something you said struck me because when you were talking about sort of the controversy with musicians and probably the audience too, about swing and bebop, that years later I read about the same thing when people talk about free or avante garde jazz, that people would say, “Yeah that’s where people go when they can’t really play.”

Well I just ignored it. Because I definitely heard that, all throughout my career. You know? And when I started doing, trying to do things, even, you know you didn’t want people to hear you making mistakes even when you practice. And you have to make mistakes when you practice, because you have to overcome those mistakes and form a discipline around them. So it just, well a lot of things. I kept quiet about it pretty much until I was at home, and then I could discuss this with my parents and my relatives, but I thought so many of these rules were just completely ridiculous. So as many of them as I could get away with I just ignored. I never had any respect for the law, as the imperative design for the way you live. Or at least what other people thought it should be. You know, because there were so many things that my teachers taught me throughout grade school and high school that I just did not believe. And I challenged this at home. I remember a high school teacher that, she was a substitute, and she made the statement — I think I was in my junior year of high school, that, “A Negro never contributes at anything to the building of this country.” You know? Which I thought was complete bullshit right then. But it encouraged me to study and find out the real history of the people who actually did build this country, which were almost all black because of slavery. You know? And there were other intellectual and artistic things that they were inventing that everybody was benefitting from and imitating that we were not getting credit for.
